passages.text: The gap argument needs a property of the derivative $q'$, rather than convexity of the spatial function $\Phi$. We establish the following analytic input before using minimality. Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be constant with value $c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, and let $X$ be its diffusion started at zero. Then $$ \begin{cases} q'''(t)\ge \dfrac1{1000c^2} \mathbb E\bigl[(c\Phi_{xx}(t,X_t))^4\bigr]>0,&c>0,\\[4pt] q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0,&c=0, \end{cases}\qquad t\in I. $$ Thus $q'$ is strictly convex for $c>0$ and strictly increasing for $c=0$. The coefficient may jump outside $I$ and may be unbounded near one, provided it is nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous and integrable. No support property or minimising assumption enters this statement. The positive-time restriction matters when a diffusion density is used; interval endpoints are handled later by continuity. [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][fs-curv]. The proof has two stages. In §§4.1–4.4 the coefficient is a positive monotone finite-step function with smooth terminal data. Shape comparisons and boundary estimates justify the [polynomial correction](#curvature-algebra) and its zero expectation. In [§4.5](#plateau-limit), approximants $\gamma_n,\Phi_n,X^n$ approach an arbitrary admissible coefficient. Only the integrated expression in spatial derivatives passes to the limit; the auxiliary forward scores need not converge. Bounds depend on a fixed compact strip and a common coefficient mass bound. The strictly positive right side is then justified for the limiting solution itself. ### 4.1 Why the uncorrected expression has no pointwise sign On a positive constant interval put $r=c\Phi_x$, $v=r_x$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. In forward time, $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$ and $dX_t=r(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t$. Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's formula gives $$ dr(t,X_t)=v(t,X_t)\,dB_t, $$ $$ dv(t,X_t)=-v(t,X_t)^2\,dt+w(t,X_t)\,dB_t, \qquad dw(t,X_t)=-3v(t,X_t)w(t,X_t)\,dt+z(t,X_t)\,dB_t. $$ Since $q'=c^{-2}\mathbb E v^2$, the drift of $v^2$ yields $c^2q''=\mathbb E(w^2-2v^3)$. The drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are, respectively, $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$. Therefore $$ c^2q'''=\mathbb E\bigl[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4\bigr]. $$ These are interior-time identities. On a smaller constant interval the heat formula gives classical time smoothness and bounded spatial derivatives of sufficiently high order, so the local martingale terms have zero mean and the expectation differentiations are justified. Nothing here assigns a sign to $q''$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][fs-reg]. There is a concrete obstruction to reading the last display pointwise. For the smooth finite-step problem $c=M=1$ on $[0,1)$, with terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$, the exact solution is $$ \Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+\frac{1-t}{2},\qquad r=\tanh x. $$ Indeed, $\Phi_{xx}+\Phi_x^2=1$. Writing $R=r^2$ gives $v=1-R$, $w=-2rv$ and $z=-2v^2+4Rv$. At $R=1/2$, $v=1/2$, $w^2=1/2$ and $z=1/2$, so $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4=-\frac{19}{8}<0. $$ This example lies in the smooth analytic class used below. Its diffusion density is $f_t(x)=e^{-t/2}\cosh(x)p_t(x)$, obtained from the heat transition formula, and integrates to one because $\mathbb E\cosh(B_t)=e^{t/2}$. It illustrates the necessity of the integration argument; it uses a smooth terminal value and makes no claim to be the zero-temperature minimiser. The displayed negative value is an exact elementary calculation. The heat formula itself is [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]. The same pointwise obstruction occurs with the actual terminal datum $|x|$. For the admissible constant coefficient $\gamma_c\equiv c>0$, write $\tau=1-t>0$ and use the same heat formula: $$ \Phi_c(t,x)=c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}. $$ At $c=0$ its continuous extension is the heat value, whose derivatives are $$ a_0=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi\tau}}e^{-x^2/(2\tau)},\qquad b_0=-\frac{x}{\tau}a_0,\qquad d_0=\left(\frac{x^2}{\tau^2}-\frac1\tau\right)a_0. $$ At $x=\sqrt\tau$, $d_0=0$ and $b_0^2=a_0^2/\tau>0$. For fixed $t,x$, Gaussian convolution may be differentiated in $x$ through its kernel and expanded in $c$ near zero: exponential moments dominate every resulting polynomial factor. The apparent singularity of $c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}$ is removable, and its spatial derivatives through order four are smooth in $c$. Hence $$ d_c^2-12c a_cb_c^2+6c^2a_c^4 =-\frac{12a_0^3}{\tau}c+O(c^2)<0 $$ for all sufficiently small positive $c$, at that fixed point. This is an ordinary consequence of the constant-coefficient formula, not an arbitrary assignment of unrelated derivative values. It neither asserts minimality of $\gamma_c$ nor contradicts the positive expectation proved below; it shows why that expectation cannot be replaced by a pointwise inequality even in the absolute-value-terminal model. ### 4.2 The smooth finite-step problem and its boundary control Take $0=t_0<\cdots ### 4.3 Backward and forward comparisons, including jumps Use backward time $\tau$ on a single step. The equation is $r_\tau=\tfrac12r_{xx}+rr_x$. The logarithmic heat formula preserves strict positivity of $v$: its second spatial derivative is the tilted mean of the old second derivative plus the tilted variance of the old first derivative. Initially $v=cM\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)>0$, and positive rescaling at a backward jump preserves this property. Consequently $r(x)>0$ for $x>0$. Twice differentiating gives $w_\tau=\tfrac12w_{xx}+rw_x+3vw$. At the terminal endpoint $w=-2cM^2\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\tanh(Mx)\le0$ for $x>0$. The boundary value at zero is zero, and the differentiated tails make the far boundary tend uniformly to zero. Comparison applied to $-w$ gives $w\le0$ on the positive half-line. Define $$ H=\frac{r_\tau}{r}=\frac{w}{2r}+v. $$ Oddness and $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$ make $w/r$, hence $H$, smooth and even at zero. Direct differentiation gives $$ H_\tau=\tfrac12H_{xx}+(v/r+r)H_x+vH, $$ $$ (H_x)_\tau=\tfrac12(H_x)_{xx}+(v/r+r)(H_x)_x +((v/r)_x+2v)H_x+wH. $$ The terminal signs are $H=(cM-M^2)\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\le0$ and $H_x\ge0$ on $x>0$, using $M\ge c$. For the first comparison write $v/r+r=1/x+\eta(x)$, where $\eta$ is smooth and odd near zero. The radial extension $H(|y|)$ to $\mathbb R^3$ turns $\tfrac12H_{xx}+x^{-1}H_x$ into $\tfrac12\Delta H$. It is smooth at the origin, as is the extra drift, and $H$ tends uniformly to zero at infinity. Comparison on expanding balls proves $H\le0$. For the second comparison, $wH\ge0$ and $(v/r)_x=w/r-v^2/r^2<0$, so the zeroth-order coefficient has upper bound $2\sup v$. On $[\varepsilon,A]$, the two lateral errors are $H_x(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon)$ and $H_x(A)=o_A(1)$, uniformly on the closed step. Taking $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and $A\to\infty$ gives $H_x\ge0$. At a backward jump $r_{\rm new}=\alpha r_{\rm old}$ with $0<\alpha\le1$, $$ H_{\rm new}=H_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)v_{\rm old},\qquad (H_x)_{\rm new}=(H_x)_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)w_{\rm old}. $$ Thus both signs survive every jump. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.2][fs-signs]. For the forward score use $a_s=s_x$, temporarily distinguishing it from the Hessian $a=\Phi_{xx}$. The forward heat equation gives $$ s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x,\qquad (a_s)_t=\tfrac12(a_s)_{xx}-s(a_s)_x-a_s^2, $$ $$ (s_{xx})_t=\tfrac12(s_{xx})_{xx}-s(s_{xx})_x-3a_s s_{xx}. $$ The first step has $s=x/t$. Thereafter $a_s-1/t$ satisfies the linear equation with drift $-s$ and zeroth-order coefficient $-(a_s+1/t)$. For fixed smooth data this coefficient is bounded above on a closed step, independently of spatial truncation; this uses the tail bound and continuity, before asserting its sign. Comparison gives $a_s\ge1/t$. The last displayed equation then gives $s_{xx}\le0$ on $x>0$. At a forward jump, $$ s_+=s_-+\delta\Phi_x,\quad (a_s)_+=(a_s)_-+\delta\Phi_{xx},\quad (s_{xx})_+=(s_{xx})_-+\delta\Phi_{xxx}. $$ The backward signs and $\delta\ge0$ preserve the forward signs. A further comparison, not concavity alone, is needed. On $x>0$ set $d_s=s_x/s$, $d_r=r_x/r$ and $\rho=d_s-d_r$. The heat equation gives $s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x$, whereas $r_t=-rH$. Taking logarithmic derivatives yields $$ (d_s)_t=\tfrac12(d_s)_{xx}+d_s(d_s)_x-s_{xx},\qquad (d_r)_t=-H_x. $$ Since $\tfrac12(d_r)_{xx}+d_r(d_r)_x=\tfrac12(w/r)_x=H_x-w$, substitution of $d_s=d_r+\rho$ gives its equation $$ \rho_t=\tfrac12\rho_{xx}+d_s\rho_x+(d_r)_x\rho +2H_x-w-s_{xx}. $$ All three terms in the source are nonnegative by the comparisons already proved, and $(d_r)_x<0$. On the first step, concavity gives $r(x)=\int_0^xv(y)\,dy\ge xv(x)$, so $\rho=1/x-v/r\ge0$. Odd Taylor expansions give $d_s=1/x+O(x)$, $d_r=1/x+O(x)$ and $\rho=O(x)$ near zero; the tail estimates give $\rho\to0$ at infinity. Comparison on $[\varepsilon,A]$ therefore proves $\rho\ge0$ on each subsequent step provided its initial sign is preserved. Define $$ j=s\rho=s_x-(s/r)v. $$ At a forward jump, with $\alpha=c_+/c_-$ and $\lambda=(c_+-c_-)/c_-$, $r_+=\alpha r_-$, $v_+=\alpha v_-$, $s_+=s_-+\lambda r_-$ and $(s_x)_+=(s_x)_-+\lambda v_-$. Substitution cancels the added terms and gives $j_+=j_-$. Since $s_+>0$ on $x>0$, the sign of $\rho$ is preserved. The quotient $s/r$ extends smoothly and evenly across zero, with $j(0)=0$; reflection gives $j\ge0$ everywhere. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.3][fs-signs]. ### 4.4 How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful Here the coefficient is a positive constant $c$ on the step containing the chosen time. The variables are the rescaled spatial derivatives $$ r=c\Phi_x,\qquad v=c\Phi_{xx},\qquad w=c\Phi_{xxx},\qquad z=c\Phi_{xxxx}. $$ Write $h=e^{c\Phi}$ and factor the forward diffusion density as $f=hg$; its auxiliary score is $s=-\partial_x\log g$. These are the backward and forward quantities compared in §4.3. On the positive half-line, where $r,s>0$, set $$ H=\frac{w}{2r}+v,\qquad j=s_x-\frac{s}{r}v,\qquad \rho=\frac{s_x}{s}-\frac vr, \qquad j=s\rho. $$ In this certificate only, $b=-w/r$ is a quotient; it is not the derivative $\Phi_{xxx}$ denoted by $b$ in the unscaled curvature formula. At a fixed positive time inside the step define $$ R=r^2,\quad K=rs,\quad b=-w/r,\quad B=b-2v, \quad L=-rs_{xx},\quad S_1=z+bv-2Rb. $$ The subscript on $S_1$ distinguishes it from the support set. The previous comparisons give $$ R,K,v,B,j,L,S_1\ge0,\qquad b=B+2v\ge0,\qquad Rb^2=w^2, $$ because $B=-2H$ and $S_1=2rH_x$. Here $s=-\partial_x\log g$ belongs to the forward heat factor, while $\partial_x\log f=r-s$ is the logarithmic derivative of the diffusion density. The signs have separate sources: $B\ge0$ comes from $H\le0$, $S_1\ge0$ from $H_x\ge0$ on the positive half-line, $j=s\rho\ge0$ from the relative-slope comparison, and $L=-rs_{xx}\ge0$ from forward concavity. Reflection extends these signs. The quotients were defined for $x>0$, where $r>0$ and $v>0$ by the tilted mean-and-variance argument in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons). At zero, $r$ and $w$ are odd, $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$, and division by $r$ is therefore division by a function with a simple zero. This gives the smooth even extension $b(0)=-z(0)/v(0)$; the other comparison identities give $j(0)=0$ and $S_1(0)=0$. Thus zero is not an omitted boundary of the integration. For $\mathcal D=r\partial_x$, direct differentiation gives $$ \mathcal D(R,K,v,b,j) =(2Rv,\ 2vK+Rj,\ -Rb,\ -z-bv,\ -jv+Kb-L). $$ Also $f_x/f=r-s$. Hence $\mathcal W(F)=\mathcal DF+(v+R-K)F$ satisfies $$ f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF). $$ This identity does not itself make the integral vanish. The tails give $r=O(1)$; exponential decay of $v,w,z,b$ and their derivatives; $s=x/t+O(1)$; $j=1/t+O((1+x)e^{-\kappa x})$; and $K=O(1+x)$. Every polynomial $F$ in $R,K,v,b,j$ and its differentiated expression therefore has at most polynomial growth. Meanwhile $f(t,x)\le C\exp(-x^2/(2t)+C|x|)$. Thus every term used below is absolutely integrable and $rfF\to0$ at both infinities. Smooth extension across zero prevents an interior boundary term. Integrating on $[-A,A]$ and taking $A\to\infty$ now gives $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.4][fs-signs]. The proof has four separate checks: the comparisons supply these signs; the tail estimates make the correction integrate to zero; the rational identity below gives a positive remainder; and [§4.5](#plateau-limit) passes the resulting expectation inequality to the original coefficient. The polynomial check verifies the third step. Set $$ (A,C,k,T_0,g_0,h_0)= \left(\frac1{13},\frac{53}{24},\frac{19}{16},\frac{73}{48}, \frac{2331}{10000},\frac{87}{2500}\right), $$ $$ (x_0,y,m,n_0)= \left(\frac{4663}{5000},\frac{6853}{10000}, -\frac{1051}{400},-\frac{1073}{500}\right). $$ Define $$ Q=Avb+Cv^2+kKv-2kRb+T_0Rv,\qquad T_1=v(g_0R+h_0j), $$ $$ \begin{aligned} F_2={}&(Av-2kR)b^2 +b\bigl(2Cv^2+2kKv+(g_0+2T_0)Rv+h_0jv\bigr)\\ &+x_0v^2j+yv^3+mKv^2+n_0Rv^2. \end{aligned} $$ The choice is motivated by the terms containing $z$. In fact, $$ \begin{aligned} \partial_bF_2 &=2(Av-2kR)b+2Cv^2+2kKv+(g_0+2T_0)Rv+h_0jv\\ &=2Q+T_1,\\ {}[z]\mathcal W(F_2)&=-\partial_bF_2=-(2Q+T_1). \end{aligned} $$ Here $[z]$ means the coefficient of $z$; only $\mathcal Db=-z-bv$ contributes it. The square $(z+Q)^2$ and $S_1T_1$ contribute $2Q+T_1$, so these terms cancel exactly. Therefore subtracting $(z+Q)^2+S_1T_1+\mathcal W(F_2)$ from the curvature expression cancels every term involving $z$. The other favourable derivative is $\partial_jF_2=x_0v^2+h_0bv\ge0$: the $-L$ in $\mathcal Dj$ leaves a nonnegative correction. Put $$ \begin{aligned} P_0&=Rj(b-7v)^2,& P_1&=RB(b-\tfrac73v)^2,\\ P_2&=Kv(b-\tfrac92v)^2,& P_3&=vB(K+\tfrac14R-\tfrac17v)^2,\\ P_4&=(vb-\tfrac{14}{5}v^2-\tfrac{13}{4}Kv+\tfrac43Rv)^2, \end{aligned} $$ $$ (p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)= \left(\frac{337}{10000},\frac{183}{2500},\frac{411}{10000}, \frac{11461}{5000},\frac{647}{10000}\right). $$ Exact expansion, with $b=B+2v$, gives $$ z^2-12Rvb^2+6v^4 =(z+Q)^2+S_1T_1+\sum_{i=0}^4p_iP_i +\mathcal W(F_2)+L(x_0v^2+h_0bv)+P_{\rm rem}. $$ For completeness, the entire remainder is specified by this table; every unlisted coefficient is zero. | Monomial | Coefficient | Monomial | Coefficient | | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | | $R^2v^2$ | $223/160000$ | $R^2vB$ | $4007/240000$ | | $R^2B^2$ | $1097/120000$ | $RKv^2$ | $83/80000$ | | $RKvB$ | $3343/24000$ | $Rv^3$ | $16259/23400000$ | | $Rv^2B$ | $30179/5460000$ | $Rv^2j$ | $26/625$ | | $RvB^2$ | $107/15000$ | $RvBj$ | $3/2500$ | | $RB^3$ | $121/32500$ | $RB^2j$ | $11/10000$ | | $K^2v^2$ | $579/20000$ | $K^2vB$ | $207/2500$ | | $Kv^3$ | $911/975000$ | $Kv^2B$ | $349/420000$ | | $Kv^2j$ | $5011/5000$ | $KvB^2$ | $133/130000$ | | $KvBj$ | $87/2500$ | $v^4$ | $1661507/1521000000$ | | $v^3B$ | $633799/621075000$ | $v^2B^2$ | $10657/1690000$ | All square prefactors $Rj,RB,Kv,vB,1$ are nonnegative, as are $S_1T_1$, $L(x_0v^2+h_0bv)$ and every remainder monomial. Integration removes only $\mathcal W(F_2)$, giving $$ \mathbb E_f[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] \ge\frac{1661507}{1521000000}\mathbb E_fv^4 \ge\frac1{1000}\mathbb E_fv^4. $$ The surplus of the first coefficient over $1/1000$ is exactly $140507/1521000000>0$. The rational identity and positive table can be checked by finite arithmetic. Their application to this diffusion also uses the signs, quotient behaviour, integrability and vanishing flux proved above. Dividing the integrated inequality by $c^2$ returns $$ \mathbb E[\Phi_{xxxx}^2-12c\Phi_{xx}\Phi_{xxx}^2 +6c^2\Phi_{xx}^4] \ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E\Phi_{xx}^4. $$ This is the unscaled estimate needed by the gap argument. Section 4.5 passes it to the original coefficient and supplies strictness for the limiting solution. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.2][fs-cert].
passages.rationale: Reconstructs the finite-step backward and forward shape comparisons, zero expected divergence, exact rational identity and integrated coercivity. The transfer to a continuous-time coefficient and its positive/zero plateau applications are now in the fixed-time-coercivity passage.

treatments.rationale: Develops the zero-expectation divergence correction with sign, quotient-extension, tail and boundary controls; positivity is established after integration, not for the uncorrected polynomial pointwise.
Displays the rational identity and complete positive remainder table; algebraic verification is one ingredient alongside the separate analytic signs and vanishing flux.
